Android Data Safety Checker

Scans your AndroidManifest.xml permissions and Gradle dependencies for known analytics/ads/crash SDKs, maps each one to a Google Play Data safety category, and checks it against a plain list of the categories you've already declared in Play Console's App content > Data safety form -- so a missing declaration doesn't cost you a policy warning or a listing taken down for an inaccurate disclosure. Everything runs in this tab; nothing is uploaded. A command-line version for CI is in the same repository (node check.mjs . --declared declared.txt).

More: why does Play flag my Data safety form, and how do I fix it? Checking a release deadline instead? Play Store Target API Level Checker checks your targetSdkVersion against Google Play's target API level enforcement requirement -- a different Play Console gate than this page.


Open your project folder, select every AndroidManifest.xml and build.gradle/build.gradle.kts (select-all works), then choose them here. Not at your project right now? instead.

No files selected yet.

2. Tick what's already declared in Play Console's Data safety form

Common questions

Why does Google Play flag my app's Data safety declaration?

Most often because a permission your app requests, or an SDK it embeds (analytics, ads, crash reporting), collects a category of data your Play Console Data safety form doesn't declare. This tool scans your AndroidManifest.xml and Gradle files for the permissions and known SDKs that imply a category, and tells you which one is missing.

Does this tool read or fill in the Play Console form for me?

No. Play Console has no public file format this tool reads from or writes to. You tell it what you've already declared (a plain list of categories, or ticking the checkboxes in the browser tool), and it compares that against what your manifest and Gradle files suggest you collect. You still make every declaration decision in Play Console yourself.

Is my project uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser tool reads the files you select using the File API and never sends them anywhere -- everything happens in memory in your tab. The CLI never makes a network call either.

Does a clean report mean Google Play will accept my declaration?

No. This is pattern-matching against known permission names and SDK dependency coordinates -- it cannot see what a permission is actually used for, dynamically loaded code, or a compiled third-party library's real behaviour, and Google can change its Data safety categories or a given SDK's practices at any time. Always confirm against Play Console's current Data safety form and each SDK's own privacy documentation before you submit.

Evidence, not a determination. This tool reports what pattern-matching found in the files you selected and what you ticked as already declared. It cannot see what a permission is actually used for, dynamically loaded code, or a third-party SDK's real runtime behaviour, and Google can add categories or change a listed SDK's practices at any time. A clean report is not a guarantee Play Console will accept your submission -- verify against Google Play's current Data safety documentation before you submit, and decide the actual collection purpose and sharing status yourself -- this tool never picks on your behalf.

missing-data-safety-declaration.html.text:
Why Google Play flags your Data safety declaration

Google Play's Data safety section (App content > Data safety in Play Console) asks every developer to declare what user data their app collects and shares, and for what purpose. Google's policy requires that declaration to be accurate -- and the most common way it stops being accurate is silent drift: a permission or a third-party SDK starts collecting a category of data that the form was never updated to mention.

What actually triggers a mismatch

Two sources, both easy to miss because neither shows up as a compile error:

SourceExampleImplied category
A requested permissionACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, READ_CONTACTS, RECORD_AUDIOLocation, Contacts, Audio files
A third-party SDKFirebase Analytics, AdMob, a crash reporter, an ad networkApp activity, Device or other IDs, App info and performance

A permission added for one feature (say, location for a store-locator screen) is trivial to forget when the Data safety form was filled in months earlier at first submission. An SDK is worse: many are added transitively by another dependency, so nobody on the team consciously chose to add data collection at all.

Find the exact gap

The checker on this site scans your AndroidManifest.xml and Gradle files for the permissions and known SDKs that imply a category, and compares the result against a plain list of what you've already ticked in Play Console -- naming the exact file and line behind anything undeclared. It runs as a browser tool (nothing uploaded) or a Node CLI you can add to your own pre-release check.

This is evidence of what the manifest, the Gradle files, and your declared list say -- not a determination that Play Console will accept the submission. See the checker and its disclaimer for what it can and can't see, and verify against Google Play's current Data safety documentation before you publish.

target-api-level.html.text:
Play Store Target API Level Checker

Reads your AndroidManifest.xml or Gradle targetSdkVersion/targetSdk declaration and checks it against Google Play's published target API level requirement -- the gate that restricts an update from reaching devices on newer Android versions once its target API level falls too far behind, separate from the Data safety declaration the sibling checker on this page covers. Everything runs in this tab; nothing is uploaded. A command-line version for CI is in the same repository (node target-sdk-check.mjs . --form-factor phone-tablet).

Select-all works for multiple files. Not at your project right now? instead.

No files selected yet.

Common questions

What happens if my app's targetSdkVersion is below Google Play's requirement?

Your app is not removed from Google Play. Instead, it stops being visible to and installable by new users on a device running a newer Android version than your app targets. Existing installs, and users on an OS version at or below your app's target, are unaffected.

Is the required target API level the same for every app?

No. Google Play sets a different floor per form factor -- phone/tablet, Wear OS, Android TV, Android XR, and Android Automotive OS each have their own required level, and a newly published app must meet a higher floor than an update to an app already on Google Play. Pick your form factor above before reading the result.

Can I get more time to meet the deadline?

Google states that an extension to the primary deadline can be requested in Play Console. This tool shows both the primary deadline and the extension deadline it has on record, but whether an extension applies to your app is only visible in your own Play Console -- this tool cannot see that.

Is my project uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser tool reads the files you select using the File API and never sends them anywhere -- everything happens in memory in your tab. The CLI never makes a network call either.

Evidence, not a determination. The deadline and per-form-factor floor above are reproduced from Google's own target API level requirement page, dated 2026-09-23. Google revises these numbers and dates on its own schedule, and whether an extension applies to your specific app is visible only in your own Play Console. A clean report here is not a guarantee Google Play will treat your app as compliant -- verify against Google's current target API level requirement page before you rely on it.

vs-manually-reviewing-play-console-warni.text:
← Android Data Safety Checker

This checker vs. guessing from Google's docs or waiting for a Play Console policy warning

Google Play's documentation names the Data safety data-type categories and what each one covers -- it is the source of truth this tool's own category list is checked against. What it does not do is read your specific AndroidManifest.xml, your specific Gradle files, or your specific declared list and tell you which category your app actually triggers, in which file, or whether your declaration already covers it. That cross-check has always meant either a guess informed by the docs, or a definite answer from a Play Console policy warning -- or a listing taken down -- after the fact.

What each approach actually gives you

Google's documentation is complete and authoritative about what the categories are and what they cover. It is not a scanner: it cannot look at your project and tell you that app/build.gradle line 6 pulls in Firebase Analytics with no matching Data safety entry, because it has never seen your code.

A Play Console policy warning will eventually tell you, with certainty -- after publishing, a policy review, and a warning naming the gap, sometimes after the listing is already live. For a category pulled in transitively by a dependency's own dependency rather than one your team added on purpose, that warning may be the first time anyone learns the SDK collects that category at all.

This checker runs the same permission-and-SDK-to-category cross-check a policy review would, against your manifest, Gradle files, and declared list, before you submit -- in the browser (nothing uploaded) or as a Node CLI you can gate CI on.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Which category does my app trigger, and where?This checker's scan -- file and line, free, nothing uploaded.
What does a given category cover?This checker lists them alongside your results; both it and Google's docs agree, since this tool's list is checked against Google's published one.
Will Play Console actually accept my declaration?Neither. Only Google's own policy review determines that -- this is evidence about your manifest, Gradle files, and declared list as they stand today.
Is my project uploaded anywhere?No. The browser tool reads files with the File API; the CLI never makes a network call.

Common questions

Doesn't Google Play's own documentation already explain this?

It lists the Data safety data-type categories and what each one covers, and it is the source of truth this tool's own category list is checked against. What it doesn't do is read your specific AndroidManifest.xml, your specific Gradle files, or your specific declared list and tell you which category your app actually triggers, in which file, on which line. That cross-check is what used to mean either guessing from the docs or finding out from a policy warning.

What does waiting for a Play Console policy warning actually cost?

At minimum, a policy-warning email and a fix-and-resubmit cycle; at worst, a listing taken down for an inaccurate Data safety disclosure while you scramble to correct it live. For a category pulled in transitively by a dependency's own dependency rather than one you added on purpose, the warning may be the first time anyone on the team learns the SDK collects that category at all. Scanning your manifest and Gradle files before you submit catches the same gap without spending a review cycle -- or a live listing -- to find it.

Can I just search my project by hand for these permissions and SDKs?

You can, and for a small project it may be faster than downloading a tool. The risk is coverage: 20-plus permissions across every AndroidManifest.xml in a multi-module project, plus every Gradle dependency coordinate a transitive library might have pulled in without anyone adding it directly. This tool runs the same permission and SDK list against every file you point it at, in the browser or as a CI-gating CLI, so a category buried in a module or a transitive dependency you didn't think to check is not the one that reaches a policy warning first.

Does a clean report from this tool replace Google Play's own review?

No, and it is not built to. This is pattern-matching against known permission names and Gradle dependency coordinates -- it cannot see what a permission is actually used for, dynamically loaded code, or a compiled third-party library's real runtime behaviour, and Google can change its Data safety categories or a listed SDK's practices at any time. A clean report means your current manifest, Gradle files, and declared list agree with each other; it is not a guarantee Play Console will accept your submission, so verify against Google's current documentation before you publish.
